name: Omar Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Hollins Farm for the Whitlow family trust. It's four hundred hectares of wheat, oilseed rape and grass, and nine hundred ewes. Most days start with checking the sheep on the quad bike, then whatever the season wants: drilling, spraying, lambing, shearing. I've got two full-timers and students in the summer. The thing I love is a field of wheat on a still evening in July, and the thing that wears me out is that the trust's accountant rings me every Thursday about costs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new tech on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Some. We got GPS steering on the big tractor three years ago, once I'd seen it work on two neighbours' farms first. I use one of those AI chat programs now and then to help write grant forms, because I hate writing them. My wife Amira teaches at the primary school and she laughs that I trust a computer to write but not to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it saved us a bit of time on forms and that's about it. At the discussion group with the other farm managers, I'd say we all got sold a lot of noise. Online I'd probably keep quiet, I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for us, which is fine. The real money pressure is fertiliser prices and the trust wanting a better return. If the AI only writes my grant forms, that's a win for my evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep using the chat program for the paperwork, and maybe try it for planning sheep rations once a couple of others in the group have. We'd keep putting a hundred and fifty a month into savings, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relieved. Relieved about what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That my job doesn't get turned upside down when Sami's starting his exams and we've still got eighteen years on the mortgage. I like steady. Steady I can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss about the bigger changes not happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a robot that walks the sheep fields at night during lambing. That I'd have bought, once I'd seen it work somewhere else. Two in the morning in March, in the rain, is when I'd welcome a machine.

S0.say: I'd tell the farm managers' discussion group that AI saved us some time on forms and that we were all sold a lot of noise. Online I'd mostly stay quiet.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for me, which is fine, because the real pressures are fertiliser prices and the trust wanting better returns. If AI only writes my grant forms, I get my evenings back.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and keeps using the chat program for paperwork, maybe trying it for sheep rations once others in his group have. Keeps saving a hundred and fifty a month.
S0.quote: Two in the morning in March, in the rain, is when I'd welcome a machine.
S0.fieldNote: Omar's approach is to let others try things first, and he says so openly. His relief is tied to family timing: his son's exams and a long mortgage. He'd still welcome a robot for night lambing checks, which shows his resistance is about proof, not principle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the farm managers need a proper conversation with the unions and the government about training. I'd say workers shouldn't carry all the cost of the change. That's what I'd say at the group and probably to the local paper if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the trust would use it to cut a full-timer. That's either Gary or Neil, and Gary's got three kids. I'd probably stay, because someone has to manage the machines and the trust, but my job would be more screens and less sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a season to see what the first farms in the area do with it. Then I'd ask the trust to pay for both full-timers to train on whatever we buy, so we keep them. I'd start using the AI tools a bit more myself, for crop planning, once I'd seen them get it right on someone else's farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for me, but I'd be dreading the conversation with Gary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the truth before the trust does. Then I'd tell him I've asked for training for him and I'll fight for it. If it went wrong I'd help him find work, there are other farms within twenty miles still hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push back on the trust if they wanted to cut a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push, yes. I'd show them the numbers, because they listen to numbers. But I wouldn't threaten to quit over it. I've got a mortgage and two kids, and I'm not a hero.

S1.say: I'd tell the discussion group and the local paper that farm managers, unions and the government need to talk about training. Workers shouldn't carry all the cost of the change.
S1.think: I think the trust would use it to cut one of my two full-timers, and Gary has three kids. I'd likely keep my job, but it would be more screens and less sheep.
S1.do: Waits a season to watch what nearby farms do, then asks the trust to pay for training for both full-timers. Starts using AI tools for crop planning once he has seen them work elsewhere.
S1.quote: I'd push, yes. I'd show them the numbers, because they listen to numbers. But I wouldn't threaten to quit over it.
S1.fieldNote: His worry is for a worker under him rather than for himself. His progressive views show in wanting workers protected, but he's frank about the limit: he won't risk his own job for it. He would still wait a season before acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that the government has to step in, now, with income support and rules on how fast farms can replace people. Two years is a disgrace if nobody's ready. I'd sign whatever petition goes round and I'd say so at the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out within a year of it arriving. The trust would buy whatever robot lambs, drills and harvests, and they'd keep someone part-time to watch it, probably a cheaper someone. My whole thing is waiting to see it proven, and in two years there's no waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the savings going into the holiday fund and put it all in the bank account, and we'd cut the second car. I'd ask Amira's school whether teaching assistants are safe, because her pay might be all we have. I'd write to our MP, and I'd look hard at whether the trust would let me rent a few fields myself, in case owning beats working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the moment you see the ewe's in trouble and the vet's an hour away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your thing is waiting for proof. What happens to that when there's no time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It breaks, basically. I'd have to jump without seeing anyone else jump first, and I'm bad at that. I'd probably jump late and land badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could the family manage if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months, maybe four. Amira's pay covers the food and the bills, but not the mortgage as well. That's the one I'd lie awake over.

S2.say: I'd tell the group and sign petitions saying the government has to step in now with income support and limits on how fast farms can replace people. Two years with nobody ready is a disgrace.
S2.think: I think I'd be out within a year of it arriving, with the trust keeping someone cheaper part-time to watch the robots. My habit of waiting for proof doesn't work when there is no time.
S2.do: Moves all savings to the bank, cuts the second car and checks whether Amira's school job is safe. Writes to his MP and asks the trust about renting a few fields himself.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like seeing a ewe in trouble with the vet an hour away.
S2.quote: I'd have to jump without seeing anyone else jump first, and I'm bad at that. I'd probably jump late and land badly.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year warning cuts straight through Omar's main coping style, which is watching others first. He sees it clearly and says he'd likely act too late. His idea of renting fields is the first sign he'd think about owning rather than working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them: training money, public support, and farm workers in the room when the rules are written. I'd say it at the group and maybe stand up at the county farming show debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to watch two or three farms go first, which is how I like it. By 2029 I'd know what works. I'd still think the trust doesn't need me in the end, but I'd have a better landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd use the AI tools properly and get the trust to trial one field robot, so I'm the one who knows it. I'd save hard, maybe three hundred a month. By year three I'd be asking whether I could rent part of the farm myself, or run the robots for several farms at once as a contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run robots for several farms. Is that a real plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hope, right now. I know two managers who'd go in with me. But I don't know if farms would pay a person to run robots if the robots can run themselves. I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami, who's starting his exams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to pick farming just because I did. Pick something where you work with people. And I'd tell him I'm sorry I can't give him better advice than that.

S3.say: I'd say at the group and the county show debate that we have a few years, so let's use them for training money, public support and workers in the room when rules are written.
S3.think: Five years lets me watch two or three farms go first, which suits me, and I'd land better. I'd still expect the trust not to need me by the end.
S3.do: Uses AI tools properly from the first year and gets the trust to trial one field robot so he becomes the person who knows it. Saves about three hundred a month and by year three explores renting land or running robots for several farms as a contractor.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way he can work with.
S3.quote: I'd tell him not to pick farming just because I did. Pick something where you work with people.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits his style: enough time to see others go first. He's honest that his contracting idea is a hope, not a plan. His advice to his son was the most emotional moment, with an apology for not knowing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if the government does its job. Retraining, a basic income for people the robots replace, proper rules. I'd say I'm hopeful but watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think ten years is long enough for me. I'm fifty-three then. I'd have watched the first wave, picked up what works, and I could be the one running the machines on Hollins or somewhere like it. I think I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not do much the first two years except keep using the AI tools more and keep an eye on the discussion group. By year four I'd get trained on the field robots, and I'd ask the trust to make my role about running them. I'd also put a bit by for Noor's university, because she'll be eighteen by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be all right. Who wouldn't be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, again, and Neil. And the students who come every summer, because those summer jobs just disappear. Nobody's going to pay a student to pick stones if a machine does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you picture from that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first lambing where I'm not in the field at two in the morning. I'd be in bed, reading a screen. I think I'd still get up and go out, just to look.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty if the government does its job, with retraining, a basic income for displaced workers and proper rules. I'm hopeful but watching.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough for me to watch the first wave, learn what works and end up running the machines on a farm like Hollins. I think I'd be all right.
S4.do: Does little for two years beyond using AI tools more and following the discussion group. By year four trains on field robots and asks the trust to reshape his role around them, while saving for his daughter Noor's university.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but more hopeful than worried.
S4.quote: I'd be in bed, reading a screen. I think I'd still get up and go out, just to look.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Omar's watch-then-follow habit works for him and he expects to come through. His concern shifts to his workers and the summer students who'd lose seasonal work. The lambing image showed he'd miss the hands-on part even if he kept his job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything about how I make decisions needs time to watch. What would help is income support that starts the day a job goes, not six months later, and someone paying for farm workers to learn the machines before they arrive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the land. Nobody asks that. If the trust owns the land and the robots, the money just goes up to them. If farmers could rent land cheaply, more of us might still be farming.

headlineQuote: If the trust owns the land and the robots, the money just goes up to them.
portrait: Omar Ito is 43 and manages Hollins Farm, four hundred hectares of crops and nine hundred ewes, for a family trust, with two full-time workers under him. He picks up new tools only once he has seen them work on neighbours' farms, uses an AI chat program now and then for grant forms, and leans towards public support and worker protection. He is calm about the plateau, worried for his worker Gary under steady change, and alarmed by two-year AGI because it leaves no time for his watch-first habit. With five or ten years he expects to learn the robots and land on his feet, though he still worries for his staff and asks who owns the land.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the way he makes decisions depends on time to watch others go first.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts the day a job goes, and someone paying for farm workers to learn the machines before they arrive.
